78-1 Introduction
79-
80-Yurinskii's coupling (Yurinskii, 1978) has proven to be an important theoretical tool for developing
81-non-asymptotic distributional approximations in mathematical statistics and applied probability.
82:For a sum S of n independent zero-mean d-dimensional random vectors, this coupling technique
83:constructs (on a suitably enlarged probability space) a zero-mean d-dimensional Gaussian vector T
84-which has the same covariance matrix as S and which is close to S in probability, bounding the
85-discrepancy S - T  as a function of n, d, the choice of norm, and some features of the underlying
86-distribution. See, for example, Pollard (2002, Chapter 10) for a textbook introduction, and Cso¨rgo¨
87-and R´ev´esz (1981) and Lindvall (1992) for background references.
88-
89-     When compared to other coupling approaches, such as the celebrated Hungarian construction
90-(Koml´os et al., 1975) or Zaitsev's coupling (Zaitsev, 1987a,b), Yurinskii's approach stands out for
91-its simplicity, robustness, and wider applicability, while also offering tighter couplings in some
92-applications (see below for more discussion and examples). These features have led many scholars
93:to use Yurinskii's coupling to study the distributional properties of high-dimensional statistical
94-procedures in a variety of settings, often with the end goal of developing uncertainty quantification
95-or hypothesis testing methods. For example, in recent years, Yurinskii's coupling has been used
96-to construct Gaussian approximations for the suprema of empirical processes (Chernozhukov
97-et al., 2014b); to establish distribution theory for non-Donsker stochastic t-processes generated in
98-nonparametric series regression (Belloni et al., 2015); to prove distributional approximations for
99:high-dimensional p-norms (Biau and Mason, 2015); to develop distribution theory for vector-valued
100-martingales (Belloni and Oliveira, 2018; Li and Liao, 2020); to derive a law of the iterated logarithm
101-for stochastic gradient descent optimization methods (Anastasiou et al., 2019); to establish uniform
102:distributional results for nonparametric high-dimensional quantile processes (Belloni et al., 2019); to
103-develop distribution theory for non-Donsker stochastic t-processes generated in partitioning-based
104:series regression (Cattaneo et al., 2020); to deduce Bernstein­von Mises theorems in high-dimensional
105-settings (Ray and van der Vaart, 2021); and to develop distribution theory for non-Donsker U-
106-processes based on dyadic network data (Cattaneo et al., 2024). There are also many other early
107-applications of Yurinskii's coupling: Dudley and Philipp (1983) and Dehling (1983) establish
108-invariance principles for Banach space-valued random variables, and Le Cam (1988) and Sheehy
109-and Wellner (1992) obtain uniform Donsker results for empirical processes, to name just a few.
110-
111-     This paper presents a new Yurinskii coupling which encompasses and improves upon all of the
112-results previously available in the literature, offering four new primary features:
113-
114-   (i) It applies to vector-valued approximate martingale data.
115-
116-  (ii) It allows for a Gaussian mixture coupling distribution.
117-
118- (iii) It imposes no restrictions on degeneracy of the data covariance matrix.
119-
120-  (iv) It establishes a third-order coupling to improve the approximation in certain situations.
121-
122-     Closest to our work are the recent paper by Li and Liao (2020) and the unpublished manuscript
123-by Belloni and Oliveira (2018), which both investigated distribution theory for martingale data using
124-Yurinskii's coupling and related methods. Specifically, Li and Liao (2020) established a Gaussian
125-2-norm Yurinskii coupling for mixingales and martingales under the assumption that the covariance
126-structure has a minimum eigenvalue bounded away from zero. As formally demonstrated in this
127-paper (see Section 3.1), such eigenvalue assumptions can be prohibitively strong in practically
128-relevant applications. In contrast, our Yurinskii coupling does not impose any restrictions on
129-covariance degeneracy (iii), in addition to offering several other new features not present in Li and
130-
131-                                                                2
132-Liao (2020), including (i), (ii), (iv), and applicability to general p-norms. In addition, we correct a
133-slight technical inaccuracy in their proof relating to the derivation of bounds in probability (see
134-Remark 2.1).
135-
136-     Belloni and Oliveira (2018) did not establish a Yurinskii coupling for martingales, but rather a
137:central limit theorem for smooth functions of high-dimensional martingales using the celebrated
138-second-order Lindeberg method (see Chatterjee, 2006, and references therein), explicitly accounting
139-for covariance degeneracy. As a consequence, their result could be leveraged to deduce a Yurinskii
140-coupling for martingales with additional, non-trivial technical work (see Appendix B for details).
141-Nevertheless, a Yurinskii coupling derived from Belloni and Oliveira (2018) would not feature (i), (ii),
142-(iv), or general p-norms, as our results do. We discuss further the connections between our work
143-and the related literature in the upcoming sections, both when introducing our main theoretical
144-results and when presenting examples and statistical applications.
145-
146-     The most general coupling result of this paper (Theorem 2.1) is presented in Section 2, where
147-we also specialize it to a slightly weaker yet more user-friendly formulation (Proposition 2.1). Our
148-Yurinskii coupling for approximate martingales is a strict generalization of all previous Yurinskii cou-
149-plings available in the literature, offering a Gaussian mixture strong approximation for approximate
150-martingale vectors in p-norm, with an improved rate of approximation when the third moments of
151-the data are negligible, making no assumptions on the spectrum of the data covariance matrix. A
152-key technical innovation underlying the proof of Theorem 2.1 is that we explicitly account for the
153-possibility that the minimum eigenvalue of the variance may be zero, or that its lower bound may
154-be unknown, with the argument proceeding using a carefully tailored regularization. Establishing a
155-coupling to a Gaussian mixture distribution is achieved by an appropriate conditioning argument,
156-leveraging a conditional version of Strassen's theorem (Chen and Kato, 2020, Theorem B.2; Monrad
157-and Philipp, 1991, Theorem 4), along with some related technical work detailed in Appendix B. A
158-third-order coupling is obtained via a modification of a standard smoothing technique for Borel sets
159-from classical versions of Yurinskii's coupling (see Lemma B.2 in the appendix), enabling improved
160-approximation errors whenever third moments are negligible.
161-
162-     In Proposition 2.1, we explicitly tune the parameters of the aforementioned regularization
163-to obtain a simpler, parameter-free version of Yurinskii's coupling for approximate martingales,
164-again offering Gaussian mixture coupling distributions and an improved third-order approximation.
165-This specialization of our main result takes an agnostic approach to potential singularities in the
166-data covariance matrix and, as such, may be improved in specific applications where additional
167-knowledge of the covariance structure is available. Section 2 also presents some further refinements
168-when additional structure is imposed, deriving Yurinskii couplings for mixingales, martingales, and
169:independent data as Corollaries 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3, respectively. We take the opportunity to discuss
170-and correct in Remark 2.1 a technical issue which is often neglected (Pollard, 2002; Li and Liao,
171-2020) when using Yurinskii's coupling to derive bounds in probability. Section 2.5 presents a stylized
172-example portraying the relevance of our main technical results in the context of canonical factor
173-models, illustrating the importance of each of our new Yurinskii coupling features (i)­(iv).
174-
175-     Section 3 considers a substantive application of our main results: strong approximation of
176-martingale empirical processes. We begin with the motivating example of canonical kernel density
177-estimation, demonstrating how Yurinskii's coupling can be applied, and showing in Lemma 3.1 why
178-it is essential that we do not place any conditions on the minimum eigenvalue of the variance matrix
179-(iii). We then present a general-purpose strong approximation for martingale empirical processes
180-in Proposition 3.1, combining classical results in the empirical process literature (van der Vaart
181:and Wellner, 1996) with our coupling from Corollary 2.2. This statement appears to be the first of
182:its kind for martingale data, and when specialized to independent (and not necessarily identically
183-distributed) data, it is shown to be superior to the best known comparable strong approximation
184-
185-                                                                3
186-result available in the literature (Berthet and Mason, 2006). Our improvement comes from using
187-Yurinskii's coupling for the -norm, where Berthet and Mason (2006) apply Zaitsev's coupling
188-(Zaitsev, 1987a,b) with the larger 2-norm.
189-
190-     Section 4 further illustrates the applicability of our results through two examples in nonparametric
191-regression estimation. Firstly, we deduce strong approximations for partitioning-based least squares
192:series estimators with time series data, applying Corollary 2.2 directly and additionally imposing
193-only a mild mixing condition on the regressors. We show that our Yurinskii coupling for martingale
194:vectors delivers the same distributional approximation rate as the best known result for independent
195-data, and discuss how this can be leveraged to yield a feasible statistical inference procedure. We also
196-show that if the residuals have vanishing conditional third moment, an improved rate of Gaussian
197-approximation can be established. Secondly, we deduce a strong approximation for local polynomial
198-estimators with time series data, using our result on martingale empirical processes (Proposition 3.1)
199-and again imposing a mixing assumption. Appealing to empirical process theory is essential here as,
200-in contrast with series estimators, local polynomials do not possess certain additive separability
201-properties. The bandwidth restrictions we require are relatively mild, and, as far as we know, they
202:have not been improved upon even with independent data.
203-
204-     Section 5 concludes the paper. Appendix A demonstrates how our coupling results can be used to
205:derive distributional Gaussian approximations (central limit theorems) for possibly high-dimensional
206-martingale vectors (Proposition A.1). This result complements a recent literature on probability and
207:statistics studying the same problem but with independent data (see Buzun et al., 2022; Lopes, 2022;
208-Chernozhukov et al., 2023; Kock and Preinerstorfer, 2024, and references therein). We also present a
209-version of this result employing a covariance estimator (Proposition A.2), enabling the construction
210:of valid high-dimensional confidence sets via a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Finally we present
211-some further results on applications of our theory to deriving distributional approximations for
212:p-norms of high-dimensional martingale vectors in Appendix A.1.
213-
214-     All proofs are collected in Appendix B, where we also include other technical lemmas of potential
215:independent interest.

250-2 Main results
251-
252-We begin with our most general result: an p-norm Yurinskii coupling for a sum of vector-valued
253-approximate martingale differences to a Gaussian mixture-distributed random vector. The general
254-result is presented in Theorem 2.1, while Proposition 2.1 gives a simplified and slightly weaker version
255-which is easier to use in many applications. We then further specialize Proposition 2.1 to three
256:scenarios with successively stronger assumptions, namely mixingales, martingales, and independent
257-data, in Corollaries 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 respectively. In each case we allow for possibly random quadratic
258-variations (cf. mixing convergence), thereby establishing Gaussian mixture couplings in the general
259-setting. In Remark 2.1 we comment on and correct an often overlooked technicality relating to the
260-derivation of bounds in probability from Yurinskii's coupling. As a first illustration of the power of
261-our generalized p-norm Yurinskii coupling, we present in Section 2.5 a simple factor model example
262-relating to all three of the aforementioned scenarios, discussing further how our contributions are
263-related to the existing literature.

547:    The closest antecedents to Corollary 2.2 are Belloni and Oliveira (2018) and Li and Liao (2020),

549-Li and Liao (2020, Theorem 1) established an explicit 2-norm Yurinskii coupling for martingales
550-under a strong assumption on the minimum eigenvalue of the martingale quadratic variation, while

556:    Corollary 2.2 improves over this prior work as follows. With respect to Li and Liao (2020),
557-our result establishes an p-norm Gaussian mixture Yurinskii coupling for martingales without any
558-requirements on the minimum eigenvalue of the martingale quadratic variation, and permits a
559:third-order coupling if 3 = 0. The first probability bound (4) in Corollary 2.2 gives the same rate of
560-strong approximation as that in Theorem 1 of Li and Liao (2020) when p = 2, with non-random ,
561-and when the eigenvalues of a normalized version of  are bounded away from zero. In Section 3.1
562-we demonstrate the crucial importance of removing this eigenvalue lower bound restriction in
563-applications involving nonparametric kernel estimators, while in Section 4.1 we demonstrate how
564-the availability of a third-order coupling (5) can give improved approximation rates in applications
565-involving nonparametric series estimators with conditionally symmetrically distributed residual
566-errors. Finally, our technical work improves on Li and Liao (2020) in two respects: (i) we employ
567-a conditional version of Strassen's theorem (see Lemma B.1 in the appendix) to appropriately
568-handle the conditioning arguments; and (ii) we deduce valid probability bounds for S - T p, as
569-the following Remark 2.1 makes clear.
570-
571-Remark 2.1 (Yurinskii's coupling and bounds in probability)
572-
573-Given a sequence of random vectors Sn, Yurinskii's method provides a coupling in the following form:
574-for each n and any  > 0, there exists a random vector Tn with P Sn - Tn >  < rn(), where
575-rn() is the approximation error. Crucially, each coupling variable Tn is a function of the desired
576-approximation level  and, as such, deducing bounds in probability on Sn - Tn requires some extra
577-care. One option is to select a sequence Rn   and note that P Sn - Tn > rn-1(1/Rn) <
578-1/Rn  0 and hence Sn - Tn P rn-1(1/Rn). In this case, Tn depends on the choice of Rn, which
579-can in turn typically be chosen to diverge slowly enough to cause no issues in applications.
580-
581-    Technicalities akin to those outlined in Remark 2.1 have been both addressed and neglected alike
582-in the prior literature. Pollard (2002, Chapter 10.4, Example 16) apparently misses this subtlety,
583-providing an inaccurate bound in probability based on the Yurinskii coupling. Li and Liao (2020)
584-seem to make the same mistake in the proof of their Lemma A2, which invalidates the conclusion of
585-their Theorem 1. In contrast, Belloni et al. (2015) and Belloni et al. (2019) directly provide bounds
586-
587-                       9
588-in oP instead of OP, circumventing these issues in a manner similar to our approach involving a
589-diverging sequence Rn.
590-
591-     To see how this phenomenon applies to our main results, observe that the second-order martingale
592:coupling given as (4) in Corollary 2.2 implies that for any Rn  ,
593-
594-                               S - T p P p1,/23p(d)2/3Rn + E[2]1/2p(d)Rn.
595-
596-This bound is comparable to that obtained by Li and Liao (2020, Theorem 1) with p = 2, albeit
597-with their formulation missing the Rn correction terms. In Section 4.1 we discuss further their
598-(amended) result, in the setting of nonparametric series estimation. Our approach using p = 
599-obtains superior distributional approximation rates, alongside exhibiting various other improvements
600-such as the aforementioned third-order coupling.
601-
602:     Turning to the comparison with Belloni and Oliveira (2018), our Corollary 2.2 again offers the
603-same improvements, with the only exception being that the authors did account for the implications
604-of a possibly vanishing minimum eigenvalue. However, their results exclusively concern high-
605:dimensional central limit theorems for vector-valued martingales, and therefore while their findings
606:could in principle enable the derivation of a result similar to our Corollary 2.2, this would require

610-B.3, and B.4); (iii) a careful truncation scheme to account for   0; and (iv) a valid third-order

701-    This simple application to factor modeling gives a preliminary illustration of the power of our
702-main results, encompassing settings which could not be handled by employing Yurinskii couplings

708-the martingale, mixingale, and weakly dependent stationary data settings.

711-3 Strong approximation for martingale empirical processes
712-
713-In this section, we demonstrate how our main results can be applied to some more substantive
714:problems in statistics. Having until this point studied only finite-dimensional (albeit potentially
715:high-dimensional) random vectors, we now turn our attention to infinite-dimensional stochastic
716-processes. Specifically, we consider empirical processes of the form
717-
718-                                                          n           f  F,
719-
720-                                          S(f ) = f (Xi),
721-
722-                                                        i=1
723-
724-with F a problem-specific class of real-valued functions, where for each f  F, the variables
725-f (X1), . . . , f (Xn) form martingale differences with respect to an appropriate filtration. We construct
726-(conditionally) Gaussian processes T (f ) for which upper bounds on the uniform coupling error
727-supfF |S(f ) - T (f )| are precisely quantified. We control the complexity of F using metric entropy
728-under Orlicz norms.
729-
730-     The novel strong approximation results which we present concern the entire martingale em-
731-pirical process (S(f ) : f  F), as opposed to just the scalar supremum of the empirical process,
732-supfF |S(f )|. This distinction has been carefully noted by Chernozhukov et al. (2014b), who
733:studied Gaussian approximation of empirical process suprema in the independent data setting
734-and wrote (p. 1565): "A related but different problem is that of approximating whole empirical
735-processes by a sequence of Gaussian processes in the sup-norm. This problem is more difficult than
736-[approximating the supremum of the empirical process]." Indeed, the results we establish in this
737-section are for strong approximations of entire empirical processes by sequences of Gaussian mixture
738:processes in supremum norm, when the data has a martingale difference structure (cf. Corollary 2.2).
739-Our results can be further generalized to approximate martingale empirical processes (including
740:mixingale empirical processes; cf. Corollary 2.1), but to reduce notation and the technical burden
741-we do not consider this extension.

1003-    In general, however, Proposition 3.1 allows for a random covariance function, yielding a coupling
1004-to a stochastic process that is Gaussian only conditionally. Such a process can equivalently be
1005-formally viewed as a mixture of Gaussian processes, writing T = 1/2Z with an operator square
1006:root and where Z is a Gaussian white noise on F independent of H0. This extension is in contrast
1007-with much of the existing strong approximation and empirical process literature, which tends to
1008-focus on couplings and weak convergence results with marginally Gaussian processes.
1009-
1010-    A similar approach was taken by Berthet and Mason (2006), who used a Gaussian coupling due to

1063-
1064-4 Applications to nonparametric regression
1065-
1066-We illustrate the applicability of our previous strong approximation results with two substantial
1067-and classical examples in nonparametric regression estimation. Firstly, we present an analysis
1068:of partitioning-based series estimators, in which we can apply the finite-dimensional result of
1069:Corollary 2.2 directly due to an intrinsic linear separability property. Secondly, we consider local
1070-polynomial estimators, this time using the stochastic process formulation in Proposition 3.1 due to
1071-the presence of a non-linearly separable martingale empirical process.
1072-

1352-     If the residuals further satisfy E 3i | Hi-1 = 0, then a third-order Yurinskii coupling delivers
1353-an improved rate of strong approximation for Proposition 4.3; this is omitted here for brevity. For
1354-completeness, the proof of Proposition 4.3 verifies that if the regression function µ(w) is  times
1355-continuously differentiable on W then supw |Bias(w)| P h. Further, the assumption that p(w) is
1356:a vector of monomials is unnecessary in general; any collection of bounded linearly independent
1357-functions which exhibit appropriate approximation power will suffice (Eggermont and LaRiccia,
1358-2009). As such, we can encompass local splines and wavelets, as well as polynomials, and also choose
1359-whether or not to include interactions between the regressor variables. The bandwidth restriction of
1360-nh3m   is analogous to that imposed in Proposition 4.1 for partitioning-based series estimators,
1361-and as far as we know, has not been improved upon for non-i.i.d. data.
1362-
1363:     Applying an anti-concentration result for Gaussian process suprema, such as Corollary 2.1 in
1364-Chernozhukov et al. (2014a), allows one to write a Kolmogorov­Smirnov bound comparing the
1365-law of supwW |µ^(w) - µ(w)| to that of supwW |T (w)|. With an appropriate covariance estimator,
1366-we can further replace T (w) by a feasible version T^(w) or its Studentized counterpart, enabling
1367-procedures for uniform inference analogous to the confidence bands constructed in Section 4.1.
1368-We omit the details of this to conserve space but note that our assumptions on Wi and i ensure
1369-that Studentization is possible even when the discretized covariance matrix has small eigenvalues
1370-(Section 3.1), as we normalize only by the diagonal entries.
1371-
1372-     In this setting of kernel-based local empirical processes, it is essential that our initial strong
1373:approximation result (Corollary 2.2) does not impose a lower bound on the eigenvalues of the
1374-variance matrix . This effect was demonstrated by Lemma 3.1 and its surrounding discussion in
1375-Section 3.1, and as such, the result of Li and Liao (2020) is unsuited for this application due to its
1376-strong minimum eigenvalue assumption. Finally, for the special case of i.i.d. data, Chernozhukov
1377-et al. (2014b, Remark 3.1) achieve better rates for approximating the scalar supremum of the
1378-t-process in Kolmogorov­Smirnov distance by bypassing the step where we first approximate the
1379-entire stochastic process (see Section 3 for a discussion), while Cattaneo and Yu (2025) obtain
1380-better strong approximations for the entire stochastic process under additional assumptions via a
1381-generalization of the celebrated Hungarian construction (Komlo´s et al., 1975; Rio, 1994).
1382-
1383-5 Conclusion
1384-
1385-In this paper we introduced as our main result a new version of Yurinskii's coupling which strictly
1386-generalizes all previously known forms of the result. Our formulation gave a Gaussian mixture
1387-coupling for approximate martingale vectors in p-norm where 1  p  , with no restrictions on
1388-the minimum eigenvalues of the associated covariance matrices. We further showed how to obtain an
1389-improved approximation whenever third moments of the data are negligible. We demonstrated the
1390-applicability of this main result by first deriving a user-friendly version, and then specializing it to
1391:mixingales, martingales, and independent data, illustrating the benefits with a collection of simple
1392-factor models. We then considered the problem of constructing uniform strong approximations for
1393-martingale empirical processes, demonstrating how our new Yurinskii coupling can be employed
1394-in a stochastic process setting. As substantive illustrative applications of our theory to some well
1395-established problems in statistical methodology, we showed how to use our coupling results for both
1396-vector-valued and empirical process-valued martingales in developing uniform inference procedures
1397-for partitioning-based series estimators and local polynomial models in nonparametric regression.
1398-At each stage we addressed issues of feasibility, compared our work with the existing literature, and
1399-provided implementable statistical inference procedures.

1614:A High-dimensional central limit theorems for martingales
1615-
1616:We present an application of our main results to central limit theorems for high-dimensional
1617-martingale vectors. Our main contribution in this section is found in the generality of our results,
1618-which are broadly applicable to martingale data and impose minimal extra assumptions. In exchange
1619-for the scope and breadth of our results, we naturally do not necessarily achieve state-of-the-art
1620:distributional approximation errors in certain special cases, such as with independent data or when
1621-restricting the class of sets over which the central limit theorem must hold. Extensions of our results
1622-to mixingales and other approximate martingales, along with third-order refinements and Gaussian
1623-mixture coupling distributions, are possible through methods akin to those used to establish our
1624-main results in Section 2, but we omit these for succinctness.
1625-
1626:     Our approach to deriving a high-dimensional martingale central limit theorem proceeds as
1627-follows. Firstly, the upcoming Proposition A.1 uses our main result on martingale coupling
1628:(Corollary 2.2) to reduce the problem to that of providing anti-concentration results for high-
1629:dimensional Gaussian vectors. We then demonstrate the utility of this reduction by employing a
1630-few such anti-concentration methods from the existing literature. Proposition A.2 gives a feasible
1631-implementation via the Gaussian multiplier bootstrap, enabling valid resampling-based inference
1632-using the resulting conditional Gaussian distribution. In Section A.1 we provide an example
1633:application: distributional approximation for p-norms of high-dimensional martingale vectors in
1634-Kolmogorov­Smirnov distance, relying on recent results concerning Gaussian perimetric inequalities
1635-(see Nazarov, 2003; Giessing, 2023; Cattaneo et al., 2025, and references therein).
1636-
1637:     We begin with some notation. Assume the setup of Corollary 2.2 and suppose  is non-random.

1722-
1723-Remark A.1 (Comparisons with the literature)
1724:The literature on high-dimensional central limit theorems has developed rapidly in recent years (see
1725-Buzun et al., 2022; Lopes, 2022; Chernozhukov et al., 2023; Kock and Preinerstorfer, 2024, and
1726:references therein), particularly for the special case of sums of independent random vectors on
1727-rectangular sets R. As a consequence, the results in this appendix are weaker in terms of dependence
1728:on the dimension than those available in the literature. This is an inherent issue due to our approach
1729-of first considering the class of all Borel sets and only afterwards specializing to the smaller class R.
1730-In contrast, sharper results in the literature, for example, directly target the Kolmogorov­Smirnov
1731-distance via Stein's method and Slepian interpolation. The main contribution of this section is
1732:therefore to obtain Gaussian distributional approximations for high-dimensional martingale vectors,
1733-a setting in which alternative proof strategies are not available.
1734-
1735-    As our final main result, we present a version of Proposition A.1 in which the covariance matrix
1736- is replaced by an estimator ^ . This ensures that the associated conditionally Gaussian vector is
1737-feasible and can be resampled, allowing Monte Carlo quantile estimation via a Gaussian multiplier
1738-bootstrap.

1877:Remark A.2 (One-dimensional distributional approximations)
1878-In our application to distributional approximation of p-norms, the object of interest Sp is a
1879:one-dimensional functional of the high-dimensional martingale; contrast this with the more general
1880-
1881-                                                   29
1882:Proposition A.1 which directly considers the d-dimensional random vector S. As such, our coupling-
1883-based approach may be improved in certain settings by applying a more carefully tailored smoothing
1884-argument. For example, Belloni and Oliveira (2018) employ a "log sum exponential" bound (see
1885-also Chernozhukov et al., 2013) for the maximum statistic max1jd Sj, along with a coupling due
1886:to Chernozhukov et al. (2014b), to attain an improved dependence on the dimension. Naturally their
1887:approach does not permit the formulation of high-dimensional central limit theorems over arbitrary
1888-classes of Borel sets as in our Proposition A.1.

 547:     The closest antecedents to Corollary 2.2 are Belloni and Oliveira (2018) and Li and Liao (2020),
 548: who also (implicitly or explicitly) considered Yurinskii's coupling for martingales. More specifically,
 549: Li and Liao (2020, Theorem 1) established an explicit 2-norm Yurinskii coupling for martingales
 550: under a strong assumption on the minimum eigenvalue of the martingale quadratic variation, while
 551: Belloni and Oliveira (2018, Theorem 2.1) established a central limit theorem for vector-valued
 552: martingale sequences employing the standard second-order Lindeberg method. As such, their proof
 553: could be adapted to deduce a Yurinskii coupling for martingales with the help of a conditional
 554: version of Strassen's theorem and some additional nontrivial technical work.
 555: 
 556:     Corollary 2.2 improves over this prior work as follows. With respect to Li and Liao (2020),
 557: our result establishes an p-norm Gaussian mixture Yurinskii coupling for martingales without any
 558: requirements on the minimum eigenvalue of the martingale quadratic variation, and permits a
 559: third-order coupling if 3 = 0. The first probability bound (4) in Corollary 2.2 gives the same rate of
 560: strong approximation as that in Theorem 1 of Li and Liao (2020) when p = 2, with non-random ,
 561: and when the eigenvalues of a normalized version of  are bounded away from zero. In Section 3.1
 562: we demonstrate the crucial importance of removing this eigenvalue lower bound restriction in
 563: applications involving nonparametric kernel estimators, while in Section 4.1 we demonstrate how
 564: the availability of a third-order coupling (5) can give improved approximation rates in applications
 565: involving nonparametric series estimators with conditionally symmetrically distributed residual
 566: errors. Finally, our technical work improves on Li and Liao (2020) in two respects: (i) we employ
 567: a conditional version of Strassen's theorem (see Lemma B.1 in the appendix) to appropriately
 568: handle the conditioning arguments; and (ii) we deduce valid probability bounds for S - T p, as
 569: the following Remark 2.1 makes clear.
 570: 
 571: Remark 2.1 (Yurinskii's coupling and bounds in probability)
 572: 
 573: Given a sequence of random vectors Sn, Yurinskii's method provides a coupling in the following form:
 574: for each n and any  > 0, there exists a random vector Tn with P Sn - Tn >  < rn(), where
 575: rn() is the approximation error. Crucially, each coupling variable Tn is a function of the desired
 576: approximation level  and, as such, deducing bounds in probability on Sn - Tn requires some extra
 577: care. One option is to select a sequence Rn   and note that P Sn - Tn > rn-1(1/Rn) <
 578: 1/Rn  0 and hence Sn - Tn P rn-1(1/Rn). In this case, Tn depends on the choice of Rn, which
 579: can in turn typically be chosen to diverge slowly enough to cause no issues in applications.
 580: 
 581:     Technicalities akin to those outlined in Remark 2.1 have been both addressed and neglected alike
 582: in the prior literature. Pollard (2002, Chapter 10.4, Example 16) apparently misses this subtlety,
 583: providing an inaccurate bound in probability based on the Yurinskii coupling. Li and Liao (2020)
 584: seem to make the same mistake in the proof of their Lemma A2, which invalidates the conclusion of
 585: their Theorem 1. In contrast, Belloni et al. (2015) and Belloni et al. (2019) directly provide bounds
 586: 
 587:                        9
 588: in oP instead of OP, circumventing these issues in a manner similar to our approach involving a
 589: diverging sequence Rn.

 1119: \begin{corollary}[Strong approximation for sums of independent vectors]%
 1120:   \label{cor:sa_indep}
 1121: 
 1122:   Assume the setup of Theorem~\ref{thm:sa_dependent},
 1123:   and suppose $X_i$ are independent given $\cH_0$,
 1124:   with $\E[X_i \mid \cH_0] = 0$.

 1126:   with $\Sigma = \sum_{i=1}^n V_i$,

 1147:   %
 1148: \end{corollary}
 1149: 
 1150: Taking $\cH_0$ to be trivial, the first inequality \eqref{eq:sa_indep_order_2}
 1151: in Corollary~\ref{cor:sa_indep} provides an $\ell_p$-norm approximation
 1152: analogous to that presented in \cite{belloni2019conditional}. By further
 1153: restricting to $p=2$, we recover the original Yurinskii coupling as presented
 1154: in \citet[Theorem~1]{lecam1988} and \citet[Theorem~10]{pollard2002user}. Thus,
 1155: in the independent data setting, our result improves on prior work as follows:
 1156: (i) it establishes a coupling to a multivariate Gaussian mixture distribution;
 1157: and (ii) it permits a third-order coupling if $\pi_3=0$.

The weakest link is now identified precisely. CMU Corollary 2.3 does not take only the manuscript’s \(\beta_N\): its second-order bound contains both the Gaussian comparison moments and the factor \(\phi_2(d)^2=2d\). The proof omits both, and under (X) alone it has not shown \(d_J/(\sqrt n\,S_J)\to0\). So the current necessary-and-sufficient claim is not justified by the cited theorem; I’m now checking whether the classical Euclidean form genuinely removes that factor or whether the statement must be weakened.

24: 1. What is coupling?
25-
26:         A coupling of two probability measures, P and Q, consists of a probability space
27-         ( , F, P) supporting two random elements X and Y , such that X has distribution P
28-         and Y has distribution Q. Sometimes interesting relationships between P and Q
29-         can be coded in some simple way into the joint distribution for X and Y . Three
30-         examples should make the concept clearer.
31-
32-<1> Example. Let P denote the Bin(n, ) distribution. As  gets larger, the distri-
33-         bution should "concentrate on bigger values." More precisely, for each fixed x, the
34:         tail probability P[x, n] should be an increasing function of . A coupling argument
35-         will give an easy proof.
36-               Consider a  larger than . Suppose we construct a pair of random variables,
37-         X with distribution P and X with distribution P, such that X  X almost
38-         surely. Then we will have {X  x}  {X  x} almost surely, from which we
39-         would recover the desired inequality, P[x, n]  P[x, n], by taking expectations
40-         with respect to P.
41:               How might we construct the coupling? Binomials count successes in inde-
42:         pendent trials. Couple the trials and we couple the counts. Build the trials from
43:   238                              Chapter 10: Representations and couplings
44-
45-   independent random variables Ui , each uniformly distributed on (0, 1). That is,
46-
47-   define X := in{Ui  } and X := in{Ui  }. In fact, the construction
48:   couples all P , for 0    1, simultaneously.

119-<3> Example. Suppose {Pn} is a sequence of probability measures on the real line,
120-         for which Pn P. Write Fn and F for the corresponding distribution functions, and
121-         qn and q for the quantile functions. From Section 7.1 we know that Fn(x)  F(x)
122-         at each x for which P{x} = 0, which implies (Problem [1]) that qn(u)  q(u) at
123-         Lebesgue almost all u in (0, 1). If we use a single U , distributed uniformly on (0, 1),
124-         to construct the variables Xn := qn(U ) and X := q(U ), then we have Xn  X almost
125-         surely. That is we have represented the weakly convergent sequence of measures by
126-         an almost surely convergent sequence of random variables.
127-
128-               Remark. It might happen that the measures {Pn} are the distributions of some
129-                 other sequence of random variables, {Yn}. Then, necessarily, Yn P; but the
130-                 construction does not assert that Yn converges almost surely. Indeed, we might even
131-                 have the Yn defined on different probability spaces, which would completely rule out
132-                 any possible thought of almost sure convergence. The construction ensures that each
133-                 Xn has marginal distribution Pn, the same as Yn, but the joint distribution of the Xn's
134-                 has nothing to do with the joint distribution of the Yn's (which is only well defined
135-                 if the Yn all live on the same probability space). Indeed, that is the whole point of
136-                 the construction: we have artificially manufactured the joint distribution for the Xn's
137-                 in order that they converge, not just in the distributional sense, but also in the almost
138-                 sure sense.
139-

 595:                  Sn   -  Wn  = Op(n-1/6)         via the Yurinskii coupling.
 596:                    n
 597: 
 598:       For k = 1, this coupling is not the best possible. For example, under an assumption
 599: 
 600:       of finite third moments, a theorem of Major (1976) gives a sequence of independent
 601: 
 602:       random variables Y1, Y2, . . ., each distributed N (0, V ), for which
 603: 
 604:                  Sn - Y1 + . . . + Yn    = op(n-1/6)          almost surely.
 605:                       n           n
 606: 
 607:       Major's result has the correct joint distributions for the approximating normals, as
 608:       n changes, as well as providing a slightly better rate.
 609: 
 610:       Example. Yurinskii's coupling (and its refinements: see, for example, the
 611:       discussion near Lemma 2.12 of Dudley & Philipp 1983) is better suited to situations
 612:       where the dimension k can change with n.
 613: 
 614:             Consider the case of a sequence of independent, identially distributed stochastic
 615:       processes {Xi (t) : t  T }. Suppose PX1(t) = 0 and |X1(t)|  1 for every t. Under
 616:       suitable regularity conditions on the sample paths, we might try to show that the
 617:       standardized partial sum processes, Zn(t) := (X1(t) + . . . + Xn(t))/ n, behave like a
 618: 10.4 The Yurinskii coupling                                                                 247
 619: 
 620: centered Gaussian process {Z (t) : t  T }, with the same covariance structure as X1.
 621: We might even try to couple the processes in such a way that supt |Zn(t) - Z (t)| is

The classical Pollard/Le Cam Euclidean theorem does not rescue (X): its parameter also carries the ambient dimension, matching CMU’s \(\phi_2(d)^2\) dependence.  2827: \subsection{Theorem-by-theorem comparison with DMAP, DPH, and MAP theory}
 2828: 
 2829: \paragraph{Theorem A (record law).}
 2830: Alfa--Neuts supply the general D-MAP construction
 2831: \cite{AlfaNeuts1995DMAP}, while M\'esz\'aros--Telek study canonical
 2832: representations for general discrete order-two MAPs and RAPs
 2833: \cite{MeszarosTelek2013DiscreteMAP2Canonical}.  Those representation results
 2834: do not assert that the present triangular, deterministically reset subfamily is
 2835: renewal.  The additional calculation here is restricted to that subfamily: it
 2836: derives the Palm gap law, increasing hazard, one-mode covariance, and exact
 2837: \(1\)-dependence criterion.  These are elementary model-specific consequences,
 2838: not a new general DMAP theorem.
 2839: 
 2840: \paragraph{Theorem B (three-inclusion quotient inverse).}
 2841: The closest prior result is the canonical-coordinate analysis of discrete
 2842: order-two MAP/RAP models by M\'esz\'aros--Telek
 2843: \cite{MeszarosTelek2013DiscreteMAP2Canonical}, together with canonical MAP2
 2844: and matrix-exponential representation work
 2845: \cite{BodrogHeindlHorvathTelek2008MAP2Canonical,
 2846: TelekHorvath2007MinimalMAP}.  That literature constructs sparse or canonical
 2847: representatives and moment-matching maps for broader representation classes.
 2848: Theorem~B neither replaces nor strengthens those canonical-form theorems.  Its
 2849: narrow additional statement is the direct rational identity
 2850: \[
 2851: \frac{r_2-r_0^2}{r_1-r_0^2}=p-b
 2852: \]
 2853: for the latched killed-reset image, which converts three visible binary
 2854: inclusion probabilities into \((p+s,ps)\) and hence the complete visible
 2855: renewal law.  The estimand is a law-determining quotient, not a labelled
 2856: minimal DMAP2 representative.  We do not claim that this identity is absent as
 2857: an implicit specialization of canonical DMAP2 coordinates; the contribution
 2858: is the explicit three-inclusion specialization and its stability bounds.
 2859: 
 2860: \paragraph{Theorems C and D (asymptotics).}
 2861: The regenerative CLT, separated-batch method, and multivariate delta method are
 2862: standard inputs \cite{Zamparo2022RenewalBinary,Janson2024RenewalCLT,
 2863: AsmussenGlynn2007,FlegalJones2010BatchMeansSpectral}.  The paper's additional
 2864: work is bookkeeping for complete retained cycles, the explicit stopped-prefix
 2865: bounds, and transport to the three-inclusion quotient.  The sorted-root and
 2866: log-rate CLTs are direct delta-method consequences and are not claimed as new
 2867: asymptotic theory.
 2868: 
 2869: \paragraph{Theorem E (projection example).}
 2870: Metric-projection limits at smooth inequality boundaries are standard
 2871: \cite{Shapiro1987MetricProjection,FangSeo2021ProjectionTests}.  Theorem~E is
 2872: therefore presented only as a pointwise worked projection at \(z_0=1/2\), with
 2873: a reproducible covariance nondegeneracy certificate.  It makes no inferential
 2874: or novelty claim beyond this specialization.
 2875: 
 2876: \paragraph{Complete-law checking and the Markov--Palm score.}
 2877: Distributional-distance consistency, serial-independence basis tests,
 2878: finite-range and Hilbert-space central limit theorems, and local Gaussian
 2879: shift calculus are standard inputs
 2880: \cite{RyabkoRyabko2010ErgodicInference,Ryabko2012StationaryTesting,
 2881: SkaugTjostheim1993SerialIndependence,DedeckerMerlevede2003HilbertCLT,
 2882: vanDerVaart1998AsymptoticStatistics}.
 2883: \Cref{thm:complete-visible-law-specification-main} combines those inputs with
 2884: the sampled-counter word law and an explicit rank-one Markov-gap path.  The
 2885: model-specific extension in
 2886: \Cref{thm:complete-markov-palm-tangent-omnibus-main} is the exact closed
 2887: interaction space obtained by adding $q(0,0)=0$ to double centring, its
 2888: $\mu^{-1}$-scaled efficient projection, and the exchange-boundary calibration
 2889: of a trace-weighted score.  It claims pointwise strict local power in every
 2890: nonzero interaction direction, but neither a new general independence test
 2891: nor a uniform infinite-dimensional minimax envelope.
 2892: 
 2893: \paragraph{Higher-state results.}
 2894: Minimal-realization uniqueness is classical, beginning with Kalman and used
 2895: directly for MAP reduction and moment matching by Telek--Horv\'ath
 2896: \cite{Kalman1963LinearSystems,TelekHorvath2007MinimalMAP}.  Accordingly,
 2897: \Cref{thm:nstate-killed-reset-identifiability-dichotomy-main} is explicitly a
 2898: recalled orbit-fibre reformulation.  The new assertion is
 2899: \Cref{thm:nstate-interior-continuum-nonidentifiability-main}: the unrestricted
 2900: interior fibre contains a positivity-preserving similarity manifold of exact
 2901: dimension \((n-1)^2\).  For serial kernels, Cumani's canonical failure-time
 2902: forms, acyclic DPH estimation, and order-two/three discrete PH canonical forms
 2903: are direct predecessors
 2904: \cite{Cumani1982CanonicalFailure,BobbioEtAl2003AcyclicDPH,
 2905: PappTelek2013DiscretePHCanonical,MeszarosPappTelek2014Traffic}.
 2906: \Cref{cor:nstate-serial-all-collision-identifiability-main} is consequently
 2907: stated as a killed-reset orbit-intersection calculation: the pure serial fibre
 2908: is exactly the rate-multiset permutation class, with collisions handled by the
 2909: confluent recurrence.  It is not claimed as a new general acyclic-DPH
 2910: canonical-form theorem.  General phase-type nonuniqueness remains fully
 2911: consistent with O'Cinneide's invariant-polytope analysis
 2912: \cite{OCinneide1989PhaseTypeNonuniqueness,OCinneide1991InvariantPolytopes}.

   3: The minimal-realization statements in this subsection are recalled background,
   4: not contributions of this paper.  Kalman's similarity theorem is the classical
   5: source, and minimal MAP/phase-type formulations and canonical-coordinate
   6: developments are given in
   7: \cite{Kalman1963LinearSystems,TelekHorvath2007MinimalMAP,
   8: BladtNielsen2017MatrixExponential,MeszarosTelek2013DiscreteMAP2Canonical,
   9: PappTelek2013DiscretePHCanonical}.  We state the consequence needed to locate
  10: the visible fibre, then prove the new quantitative assertion: at a minimal
  11: interior killed-reset kernel the admissible fibre has local dimension
  12: \((n-1)^2\).  Nonunique MAP and Coxian representatives are documented in
  13: \cite{RamirezCoboLilloWiper2010MAP2Nonidentifiability,
  14: RamirezCoboLillo2012WeakEquivalentMAP,RizkBurkeWalsh2019CoxianNonuniqueness}.
  15: Graph-specific time-to-event inverses are treated algebraically by

  17: criterion below instead isolates the exact orbit fibre for any declared
  18: minimal killed-reset subclass.

  20: \paragraph{Recalled minimal-realization uniqueness.}
  21: Let \((a,A,b)\) and \((\widetilde a,\widetilde A,\widetilde b)\) be two real
  22: scalar realizations of the same dimension \(n\) such that
  23: \[
  24: aA^k b=\widetilde a\widetilde A^k\widetilde b
  25: \qquad(k\ge0).
  26: \]
  27: Assume that both reachability matrices
  28: \[
  29: [\,b,Ab,\ldots,A^{n-1}b\,],\qquad
  30: [\,\widetilde b,\widetilde A\widetilde b,\ldots,
  31: \widetilde A^{n-1}\widetilde b\,]
  32: \]
  33: and both observability matrices
  34: \[
  35: \begin{bmatrix}a\\aA\\\vdots\\aA^{n-1}\end{bmatrix},
  36: \qquad
  37: \begin{bmatrix}\widetilde a\\\widetilde a\widetilde A\\\vdots\\
  38: \widetilde a\widetilde A^{n-1}\end{bmatrix}
  39: \]
  40: have rank \(n\). Then there is a unique \(M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\RR)\)
  41: such that
  42: \[
  43: \widetilde a=aM,
  44: \qquad \widetilde A=M^{-1}AM,
  45: \qquad \widetilde b=M^{-1}b.
  46: \]
  47: These rank hypotheses are precisely properties \textup{(R)} and \textup{(L)}
  48: of Bladt and Nielsen, whose Theorem~4.2.16 characterizes minimality by their
  49: simultaneous validity; the corresponding intertwining relations are given in
  50: their Lemmas~4.2.5--4.2.6
  51: \cite[Theorem~4.2.16, p.~216, and Lemmas~4.2.5--4.2.6,
  52: p.~212]{BladtNielsen2017MatrixExponential}. This standard result is invoked
  53: here and is not claimed as a new theorem; see also Kalman
  54: \cite{Kalman1963LinearSystems}, Telek--Horv\'ath
  55: \cite{TelekHorvath2007MinimalMAP}, and
  56: \cite{Ryden1996Aggregated,OCinneide1989PhaseTypeNonuniqueness,
  57: OCinneide1991InvariantPolytopes}.
  58: 
  59: \begin{proposition}[Recalled orbit-fibre consequence of minimal realization]
  60: \label{thm:nstate-killed-reset-identifiability-dichotomy-main}
  61: Fix \(n\ge2\), put \(\beta=e_n^\top\), and let
  62: \[
  63: \mathcal K_n=\{K\in\RR^{n\times n}:K\ge0,\ K\mathbf1\le\mathbf1,\
  64: \operatorname{spr}(K)<1\}.
  65: \]
  66: For \(K\in\mathcal K_n\), define the killed-reset D-MAP by
  67: \[
  68: T_0=K,\qquad T_1=(I-K)\mathbf1\beta
  69: \]
  70: and its Palm survival coordinates by \(S_k(K)=\beta K^k\mathbf1\).
  71: Call \(K\) minimal when both
  72: \[
  73: \mathcal C(K)=[\,\mathbf1,K\mathbf1,\ldots,K^{n-1}\mathbf1\,],
  74: \qquad
  75: \mathcal O(K)=
  76: \begin{bmatrix}\beta\\ \beta K\\ \vdots\\ \beta K^{n-1}\end{bmatrix}
  77: \]
  78: have rank \(n\). Let
  79: \[
  80: \mathcal G_n=\{M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\RR):
  81: M\mathbf1=\mathbf1,\ \beta M=\beta\},
  82: \]
  83: and let \(\mathfrak P_n\subset\mathcal G_n\) be the reset-preserving
  84: permutation matrices.
  85: 
  86: For any declared subclass \(\mathcal C\subset\mathcal K_n\) of minimal
  87: kernels, fix the structural equivalence \(\sim_{\mathcal C}\) under which
  88: identification is requested, and assume that \(K\sim_{\mathcal C}L\) implies
  89: equality of visible laws. Examples are reset-preserving hidden-state
  90: relabeling and, in a serial rate chart, permutation of the rate coordinates.
  91: Define the Markovian orbit fibre
  92: \[
  93: \mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}(K)=
  94: \left\{M^{-1}KM\in\mathcal C:M\in\mathcal G_n\right\}
  95: \big/\!\sim_{\mathcal C}.
  96: \]
  97: Then standard minimal-realization uniqueness gives the following exact
  98: characterization.
  99: \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 100: \item Two minimal kernels \(K,L\in\mathcal K_n\) generate the same stationary
 101: visible click law if and only if
 102: \[
 103: \begin{aligned}
 104: L&=M^{-1}KM &&\text{for the unique }M\in\mathcal G_n\\
 105: &&&\text{implementing their normalized minimal realizations}.
 106: \end{aligned}
 107: \]
 108: \item Equivalently, the declared hidden object is identifiable from the visible law within
 109: \(\mathcal C\), modulo \(\sim_{\mathcal C}\), if and only if
 110: \[
 111: \#\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}(K)=1\qquad\text{for every }K\in\mathcal C.
 112: \]
 113: Pointwise identifiability at \(K\) is equivalent to the same condition at
 114: that \(K\); if the cardinality exceeds one, its distinct classes are exactly
 115: the hidden nonidentifiability fibre. Thus this assertion is the orbit-fibre
 116: reformulation of part \textup{(i)}.
 117: \end{enumerate}
 118: Part~\textup{(ii)} is deliberately recorded only as terminology: after the
 119: fibre has been defined, singleton fibre and identifiability modulo
 120: \(\sim_{\mathcal C}\) are the same assertion.  Neither part is claimed as a
 121: new realization theorem.
 122: \end{proposition}
 123: 
 124: \begin{proof}
 125: Deterministic reset makes the visible process renewal. Its Palm gap tail is
 126: exactly \(S_k(K)\), so equality of visible stationary laws is equivalent to
 127: equality of all the scalar coordinates \(\beta K^k\mathbf1\), \(k\ge0\).
 128: Apply the minimal-realization theorem stated above to the triples
 129: \((\beta,K,\mathbf1)\) and \((\beta,L,\mathbf1)\). Its hypotheses are exactly
 130: the two displayed rank conditions in the proposition, and it gives a unique
 131: similarity \(L=M^{-1}KM\). Preservation of the fixed input and output vectors
 132: gives \(M\mathbf1=\mathbf1\) and \(\beta M=\beta\), respectively.
 133: Conversely, these two identities give
 134: \[
 135: \beta(M^{-1}KM)^k\mathbf1=\beta K^k\mathbf1
 136: \]
 137: for every \(k\), proving (i). Taking the intersection with
 138: \(\mathcal C\) and then quotienting precisely the declared structural
 139: equivalence proves
 140: the necessary-and-sufficient assertion (ii).
 141: \end{proof}
 142: 
 143: \begin{corollary}[All-collision serial identifiability]
 144: \label{cor:nstate-serial-all-collision-identifiability-main}
 145: Fix \(n\ge2\), a known \(\Delta\tau>0\), and arbitrary positive rates
 146: \(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\), with repetitions allowed. Let
 147: \[
 148: Q(\theta)_{ii}=-\theta_i,\qquad
 149: Q(\theta)_{i,i-1}=\theta_i\quad(2\le i\le n),
 150: \]
 151: with all other entries zero, and put
 152: \[
 153: T_0(\theta)=e^{\Delta\tau Q(\theta)},\qquad
 154: T_1(\theta)=(I-T_0(\theta))\mathbf1e_n^\top.
 155: \]
 156: Then the visible record identifies exactly the unordered rate multiset
 157: \(\{\!\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n\}\!\}\). Equivalently, the fibre of the
 158: labelled serial parameter is its \(\mathfrak S_n\)-permutation orbit.
 159: 
 160: More explicitly, if the distinct rates are
 161: \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r\) with multiplicities
 162: \(m_1,\ldots,m_r\), and \(z_j=e^{-\lambda_j\Delta\tau}\), then the Palm tail
 163: has the confluent Prony form
 164: \[
 165: S_k=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{\ell=0}^{m_j-1}
 166: c_{j\ell}k^\ell z_j^k,\qquad c_{j,m_j-1}\ne0,
 167: \]
 168: and its minimal recurrence polynomial is
 169: \[
 170: \chi_\theta(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r(x-z_j)^{m_j}.
 171: \]
 172: The leading \(n\times n\) Hankel matrix
 173: \((S_{i+j})_{0\le i,j<n}\) is invertible; hence
 174: \(S_0,\ldots,S_{2n-1}\) determine \(\chi_\theta\), including all collision
 175: multiplicities. Pole collision therefore changes conditioning and the local
 176: root chart, but does not change population identifiability.
 177: \end{corollary}
 178: 
 179: \begin{proof}
 180: Starting in phase \(n\), the absorption time is
 181: \(W=X_n+\cdots+X_1\), where the \(X_i\) are independent exponentials with
 182: rates \(\theta_i\). Its Laplace transform is
 183: \[
 184: \EE e^{-sW}=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\theta_i}{s+\theta_i}.
 185: \]
 186: Consequently
 187: \[
 188: \int_0^\infty e^{-st}\PP(W>t)\,dt
 189: =\frac{1-\prod_{i=1}^n\theta_i/(s+\theta_i)}{s}
 190: \]
 191: has at
 192: \(-\lambda_j\) a pole of exact order \(m_j\). Partial-fraction inversion and
 193: sampling at \(t=k\Delta\tau\) give the displayed exponential-polynomial form
 194: with nonzero top confluent coefficient. Standard confluent Prony algebra
 195: then gives the exact minimal annihilator \(\chi_\theta\)
 196: \cite{KunisRoemerVonDerOhe2020Prony}.
 197: 
 198: For completeness of the finite-coordinate assertion, the matrices
 199: \(\mathcal O(Q)\) and \(\mathcal C(Q)\) are nonsingular: successive rows
 200: \(e_n^\top Q^j\) and successive columns \(Q^j\mathbf1\) expose the nonzero
 201: bidiagonal products triangularly. Because the exponential is injective on
 202: the real spectrum of \(Q\), Hermite interpolation supplies a polynomial
 203: \(p\) with \(Q=p(e^{\Delta\tau Q})\); hence the corresponding observation and
 204: reachability spaces for \(T_0=e^{\Delta\tau Q}\) are also full. Therefore
 205: \[
 206: (S_{i+j})_{0\le i,j<n}=\mathcal O(T_0)\mathcal C(T_0)
 207: \]
 208: is invertible, and the first \(2n\) tails solve uniquely for the order-\(n\)
 209: recurrence. The roots and their algebraic multiplicities recover
 210: \(\lambda_j=-\Delta\tau^{-1}\log z_j\) and \(m_j\). Conversely, permuting
 211: the independent summands does not change \(W\), the Palm gap law, or the
 212: stationary renewal law. This proves the exact fibre claim.
 213: \end{proof}
 214: 
 215: \begin{theorem}[Quantitative interior fibre dimension and positivity persistence]
 216: \label{thm:nstate-interior-continuum-nonidentifiability-main}
 217: For the unrestricted class with \(\sim_{\mathcal K_n}\) equal to
 218: reset-preserving state relabelling, the hidden kernel is locally
 219: nonidentifiable at every minimal interior point \(K\), where interior means
 220: \(K>0\) and \((I-K)\mathbf1>0\) entrywise. More precisely, the
 221: reset-preserving similarity group has Lie algebra
 222: \[
 223: \mathfrak g_n=\{B:B\mathbf1=0,\ \beta B=0\},
 224: \qquad \dim\mathfrak g_n=(n-1)^2,
 225: \]
 226: and the orbit map
 227: \[
 228: \psi_K:\mathcal G_n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{n\times n},\qquad
 229: \psi_K(M)=M^{-1}KM,
 230: \]
 231: has injective differential
 232: \[
 233: D\psi_K(I)B=[K,B]\qquad(B\in\mathfrak g_n).
 234: \]
 235: Consequently the visible fibre through \(K\) contains, in a neighbourhood of
 236: \(K\), a smooth immersed manifold of dimension exactly \((n-1)^2\).  Every
 237: kernel on a sufficiently small neighbourhood of this orbit manifold remains
 238: strictly substochastic: its entries and killing deficits are positive.  After
 239: quotienting by the finite reset-preserving permutation group, the local fibre
 240: still has dimension \((n-1)^2\).
 241: \end{theorem}
 242: 
 243: \begin{proof}
 244: Because \(\beta\mathbf1=1\),
 245: \(\RR^n=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\oplus\ker\beta\).  Relative to this
 246: decomposition, \(B\mathbf1=0\) removes the first block column and
 247: \(\beta B=0\) forces the range into \(\ker\beta\).  Thus
 248: \(B=\operatorname{diag}(0,A)\), with arbitrary
 249: \(A\in\operatorname{End}(\ker\beta)\), and
 250: \(\dim\mathfrak g_n=(n-1)^2\).
 251: 
 252: Differentiating \(\exp(-tB)K\exp(tB)\) at zero gives
 253: \(D\psi_K(I)B=[K,B]\).  Suppose \([K,B]=0\).  Since \(B\mathbf1=0\),
 254: \[
 255: BK^j\mathbf1=K^jB\mathbf1=0,
 256: \qquad j=0,\ldots,n-1.
 257: \]
 258: The reachability matrix
 259: \([\mathbf1,K\mathbf1,\ldots,K^{n-1}\mathbf1]\) has rank \(n\), so these
 260: equalities imply \(B=0\).  Hence the differential is injective on all of
 261: \(\mathfrak g_n\), not merely in one selected direction.
 262: 
 263: The constant-rank theorem now makes the image of \(\psi_K\) near the identity
 264: a smooth immersed manifold of dimension \((n-1)^2\).  For every
 265: \(M\in\mathcal G_n\),
 266: \[
 267: \beta\psi_K(M)^j\mathbf1=\beta K^j\mathbf1\qquad(j\ge0),
 268: \]
 269: so the recalled orbit-fibre result places this entire manifold in the visible
 270: fibre.  Finally, all entries of \(M^{-1}KM\) and all components of
 271: \((I-M^{-1}KM)\mathbf1\) depend continuously on \(M\).  Their values at
 272: \(M=I\) are strictly positive; a sufficiently small identity neighbourhood
 273: therefore remains inside the interior Markovian cone.  The stabilizer has zero
 274: Lie algebra by injectivity of the differential, and quotienting by the finite
 275: reset-preserving permutation group cannot change local dimension.  This proves
 276: all assertions.
 277: \end{proof}
 278: 
 279: \begin{remark}[Nonminimal and graph-specific open interfaces]
 280: \label{rem:nstate-identifiability-open-interfaces-main}
 281: The characterization and the two headline results deliberately assume
 282: Hankel/minimal rank \(n\). If a nominal
 283: \(n\)-state representation has lower visible rank, equal laws need not be
 284: related by an invertible \(n\times n\) similarity; a sharp classification then
 285: requires a stratified treatment of nonminimal augmentations. For a fixed
 286: nonserial zero pattern on the boundary of the Markovian cone, evaluating the
 287: orbit intersection \(\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}(K)\) is an exact semialgebraic
 288: problem, but no graph-uniform closed form is claimed here. Finally, collision
 289: multiplicity is population-identifiable in the serial model but statistically
 290: singular under noisy finite records. These are explicit interfaces, not
 291: consequences of the present results.
 292: \end{remark}
 293: 
 294: For orientation, the unrestricted fibre is already nontrivial in two states:
 295: \[
 296: K=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\1/2&1/4\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 297: M=\begin{pmatrix}9/10&1/10\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 298: M^{-1}KM=\begin{pmatrix}9/20&1/45\\9/20&3/10\end{pmatrix}.
 299: \]
 300: Both kernels are nonnegative and substochastic,
 301: \(M\mathbf1=\mathbf1\), \(e_2^\top M=e_2^\top\), and their entire visible
 302: renewal laws coincide, although the hidden kernels do not.

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" â‰  comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after â‰  TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc â‰  systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code â†’ test exists and failed first
Otherwise â†’ not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.
